actions.justification: First priority is ensuring the safety of the environment for both patient and staff before proceeding with any clinical assessment or intervention.
Mandatory action to obtain baseline vital signs and confirm current patient hemodynamic status at time of arrival.
Mandatory action to identify any underlying medical causes (e.g., metabolic, neurological, infectious) contributing to the patient's presentation before initiating treatment.

Mandatory action: Verbal de-escalation is the first-line intervention for agitated or behaviorally disturbed patients, prioritizing least-restrictive approach before any pharmacological or physical intervention.
Mandatory action: Hypoglycemia is a common reversible medical cause of altered behavior/agitation and must be ruled out immediately as it is rapidly treatable.

Optional but clinically important: Formally assessing the aggression level guides the appropriate level of intervention (verbal, pharmacological, or physical restraint) and helps monitor response to de-escalation efforts.

Patient has had initial safety and medical assessment completed. Substance use assessment is a critical next step to identify potential toxidromes or withdrawal syndromes that may be driving the presentation, guiding appropriate management.
Following initial assessment, selecting an appropriate medication (e.g., for agitation, toxidrome, or underlying condition) is indicated based on the clinical picture emerging from the workup so far.
Verbal de-escalation should be maintained as an ongoing least-restrictive intervention while further assessment and treatment decisions are being made, consistent with safe patient care principles.
Patient safety must be maintained using the least restrictive means necessary given the context of aggression assessment and de-escalation attempts already completed.
Documentation of clinical indication for any restraint is mandatory for legal, ethical, and quality compliance purposes.

If serotonin syndrome is suspected (given the workup trajectory including substance use assessment and medical cause evaluation), cyproheptadine is first-line pharmacological treatment as a serotonin antagonist.

Benzodiazepines are first-line pharmacological treatment for agitation and can also help with serotonin syndrome symptoms by reducing neuromuscular excitability. Lorazepam is preferred over antipsychotics in this context.
IV fluid resuscitation supports hemodynamic stability and renal protection, particularly important if there is concern for hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, or serotonin syndrome.

Given the complexity of the presentation (possible serotonin syndrome, agitation requiring restraints, cyproheptadine already administered), ICU-level monitoring is warranted for close observation and management.
